b: Alena Niehaus’ Instagram feed isn’t just ASMR; it’s a way to learn more about Dallas. The urban artist takes her sketchbook to some of the most iconic (or underappreciated) spots in the city, telling their stories as she sketches them. Learn about the Filter Building, Sons of Hermann Hall, and Garland’s only museum.

From their start in 1980 as 30 men singing at Holy Trinity Catholic Church, the chorus has grown into a 250-member ensemble that continues to dazzle audiences. Today, the primarily gay male chorus boasts more than 38 albums and two documentaries, including one Emmy win.

n: DALLAS MUSEUM OF NATURAL HISTORY'S WILDLIFE DIORAMAS
b: The wildlife dioramas at the former Dallas Museum of Natural History were stored away when the museum closed in 2012. But just in time for FIFA Fan Fest in Fair Park, the detailed habitat exhibits, as haunting and bizarre as good dioramas should be, reappeared for the world’s visitors and remained up through September.

When the Dallas Opera’s lead in Don Carlo was taken down by allergies, opera staffhad mere hours to find a substitute. Singer Arturo Chacón Cruz flew in from Miami with minutes to spare and brought true beauty despite walking onstage without any rehearsal—an all-around effort that earns a bravo.

This nonprofit newsroom celebrated its first birthday in July, and in that year the team— which consists of D Magazine alum Matt Goodman and former Dallas Morning News reporters Sharon Grigsby, Kelli Smith, and Claire Ballor—has covered our city’s broken foster care system with unmatched rigor.

What do two lawyers have to do with raising up local music talent? Joe Morrison and Shane Mullen of law firm Mullen & Mullen wanted to do more with their money, so they launched the free, weeklong Jambaloo music festival which fills venues from Deep Ellum to Fort Worth, and added a music prize that gives an up-and-comer a $20,000 boost.

Willis has been a member of Dallas Theater Center’s resident acting company since 2021, stealing scenes with his emotional depth, clear tenor, and impeccable comedic timing. Whether playing the lead in Joseph and the Amazing Technicolor Dreamcoat or a supporting role in AChristmas Carol , Willis is guaranteed to captivate.

Last December marked the 50th year that homeowners in Arlington’s Interlochen neighborhood prepared light displays so over the top that families from far and wide drove in by the carload to see them. Once ranked on People magazine’s list of top 10 Christmas light displays, the free event lasts for two weeks and ends on Christmas Day.
a: Westwood Dr. at Randol Mill Rd.

b: Since its founding in 1982, the Texas International Theatrical Arts Society has brought Mikhail Baryshnikov, the Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater, MOMIX, STOMP, and more massive names in the dance world to Dallas. But somehow, its progressive programming remains an insider Arts District secret.

What began in 1979 as a storefront theater next to a downtown Fort Worth sandwich shop has grown into a theatrical force off Vickery Boulevard known for productions that both comfort and challenge. Yes, it’s worth the long drive west, especially if you’re dining in the Lobby Café before curtain.

c: Best Place to Watch the Dallas Holiday Parade
b: For princes: book a room at the Adolphus for a breakfast buffet and bleacher seating. For paupers: arrive in pre dawn hours to unfold your chairs on the south side of Commerce, across from the legendary hotel. Either way, you’ll get to see every televised performance before popping into the hotel lobby for an after-party.

Fort Worth’s Leon Bridges was on our list of 25 Most Influential Recording Artists, and his new album has only added to his artistic weight. Happiness Anytime is a collaboration with Brits Josh Lloyd-Watson and Lydia Kitto of Jungle and blends Bridges’ signature soulful style with a danceable mix of Afrobeat, Brazilian grooves, and disco.
st: Leon Bridges announces new album with Jungle

b: A kidnapped woman who’s possibly possessed. Lewis Carroll’s iconic White Rabbit. A flighty flapper entangled in a love... hexagon? All in a season’s work for Lazarchick, who is also an artistic associate at Second Thought Theatre. With a résumé so varied, the girl next door has proven she’s anything but predictable.

n: CITY RINK AT MAIN STREET GARDEN PARK
b: Downtown Dallas Inc. and CultureMap paired up to drop a temporary ice skating rink in Main Street Garden Park during the holiday season. While the weather wasn’t always cold (hello, 80-degree Christmas), the chance to hit the ice downtown, surrounded by high-rises, still made for core-memory moments.

Music directors are often the unsung heroes, but Bowling has been making everything from Assassins to Waitress sound its best at theaters all over town for the past two decades. Whether she’s wielding a baton or tickling the ivories, conducting the choir or leading the band, Bowling deserves a standing O.

If you visited the downtown park during any World Cup game, you found a mix of fans in, say, Argentine and Egyptian jerseys, slapping tables and cheering the game playing on a massive screen as kids ran between the playground and splash pad. If bringing all kinds together is a park’s goal, this one wins.

Months after The Odyssey’ s release, this North Dallas multishowings in its IMAX 70 mm theater, a format that allows larger, clearer images, literally showing audiences more of the film. Only about 25 theaters in the nation are equipped with this tech. It’s an experience worth planning ahead for.

OK2BX (“OK to be extraordinary”) allows student filmmakers from around the globe to show their work on the big screen, often for the first time ever. Founded in 2021 by Brent and Chris Bolding to honor their daughter who died by suicide after coming out as trans, the fest celebrates the creative visionaries of our future.

After a decade away, gallerist Wanda Dye returned to Dallas this year and opened a collaborative space in East Dallas with designer Stefania Morandi. The gallery is guided by an oldschool manifesto, including the tenet to “democratize collecting” with work by art stars of the local scene, sold at affordable prices.

It ignited an outsize outrage when one of mural artist Robert Wyland’s Whaling Walls, which had been on display in downtown Dallas since 1999, was covered in bright blue paint to make space for a FIFA ad. But then a tiny new addition in one corner, thanks to an anonymous graffiti writer who spraypainted a killer whale, so labeled, helped put everything back in perspective. Who says civil discourse is dead?

Since 2023, Tureen has quietly crafted a refined, ambitious program in Oak Cliff. Highlighting under-the-radar artists, the gallery keeps a special focus on queer and Indigenous makers, such as museum darling Sonya Kelliher-Combs, who has shown at the Whitney. Tureen’s Cody Fitzsimmons and Christopher Scott also promote their Dallas project at art fairs around the country.

It’s tempting to think that The Colony’s mega entertainment complex, anchored by Nebraska Furniture Mart and a Ferris wheel, is not for you. But then you’ll see a concert at Windmills, do a sauna circuit at WorldSprings, watch a basketball game at Cosm, and realize it’s Warren Buffett’s world, baby.

In an unlikely collaboration between artists and a medical foundation, this annual show takes place in a Swiss Avenue mansion, the Historic Aldredge House Museum. Organizer-artists Joel Murray, who is also the house’s caretaker, and Clint Bargers founded the project in 2022, inviting artists to site works within the house for a much-anticipated, one-weekend-only experience each fall.

You’re at your wit’s end after having been served yet another Alo-clad influencer talking about the hottest restaurant in Dallas. Then the algorithm throws you a bone and serves up Michael Harky, living his deeply normal 9-to-5 life out loud. Even Noah Kahan once commented, “God damn right.”

After running gallery spaces elsewhere, Dallas native Tessa Granowski returned to the city two years ago to open Nature of Things, a nomadic gallery. As part of her excellent programming, she has been spotlighting little-known or forgotten lore about Texan artists, musicians, and writers. As Larry McMurtry said: “Texas is rich in unredeemed dreams.”

You’ve probably seen Le’s work around town. Her hand has touched Meridian, Bar Sardine, and countless other walls and windows, leaving behind impossibly straight lines, large-scale murals, or intricate gold-leaf lettering. The videos of her process are mesmerizing.

Step 1: rename AT&T Stadium for the World Cup. Step 2: slap badly needed curtains over the windows on the west end. (Take notes, Jerry Jones.) Step 3: replace the turf with gorgeous natural grass. Step 4: bring in the rowdiest fans from across the globe, and throw the year’s best sports party.

What began as a small zine fest at Dallas Contemporary, in 2022, has grown into a dynamic celebration of art and printed matter. Founded by tattoo artist and illustrator Gino Dal Cin, who also serves as the director of operations at DC, this free multiday event brings together publishers, writers, artists, and speakers to champion books as curatorial spaces.

Sure, the event is a place to buy, sell, and trade sought-after kicks, vintage tees, and locally branded stoner’s kits and hoodies. But more than that, it’s a place where sneakerheads and streetwear enthusiasts can gather as a community—with a DJ spinning, naturally.

The 37-year-old is legend Eric Nadel’s heir apparent as the voice of the Rangers. He’s as versatile as it gets, bouncing from radio to television to the internet, and as liable to drop obscure stats on social media as line dance with cheerleaders on the dugout roof.

Tony McDowell, an Oak Cliffnative, has outworked the local competition, releasing 48 studio tracks in the last 18 months. He credits that work ethic to his mother, Sadetra, who had successful hairstyling businesses in Dallas and Houston. Only fitting, then, that his latest record, the 17-track Sadetra Son , is a tribute to her.

Just as Klyde Warren Park was built over Woodall Rodgers to bridge Uptown and downtown, this $300 million, 5-acre deck park connects parts of South Dallas and Oak Cliffthat were divided by I-35 in the 1950s. Already it bustles with yoga, food fests, and a bevy of parent-and-baby classes.

It’s impressive enough that the 19-yearold from Maine became the first rookie since Michael Jordan to lead his team in points, rebounds, assists, and steals. That he did so while restoring hope to Mavs fans heartbroken from losing Luka Dončić is miraculous. He is Dallas’ next sports icon.

When Fanny Kerwich, an eighthgeneration French circus performer, fell head over heels for a Dallas lawyer while she was touring with Barnum, her beau vowed to run away with her. Instead, Kerwich planted roots and set up her own big top in Dallas in 2006, recruiting and nurturing jaw-dropping acrobats, jugglers, clowns, and aerialists ever since.

The Kim Gordon of Dallas art institutions, The Power Station celebrates 15 years as the most discordant, rule-breaking exhibition space in town. With a mission to show challenging exhibitions with international and regional artists, this art space offers many things: awe, confusion, and sometimes wet shoes or ringing ears, but always discovery.

The trio that has done The Ticket’s morning radio show for 30 years— George “Jub Jub” Dunham, Craig “Junior” Miller, and Gordon “No Pants” Keith—are Texas Radio Hall of Famers and national Marconi winners. They launched this podcast last year because they are … hot dog?

The TEA has taken over seven districts. Meanwhile, Dallas ISD has momentum. That’s due in large part to the superintendent. She is adept at placing the right people in the right roles to improve outcomes. That comes from walking halls and talking to teachers and principals, not just sitting in her office.

n: BOOKER T. WASHINGTON'S FLYING HORSE FESTIVAL
b: This school year, Booker T. celebrates 50 years since desegregation led to its transformation into what is now one of the most renowned arts magnets in the country. The Flyinghorse Festival showcases students’ exceptional talent while raising funds for kids who can’t afford cellos and other tools of the trade. Take tissues.

Every weekday morning at 9 people who genuinely seem to enjoy each other, Ron Corning and Miranda Suarez, spend an hour talking about local new s and interviewing the people who make it. It’s a welcome salve on the wound c reated by Krys Boyd (und erstandably) thinking more about national topics.

If you own a five-figure bicycle and have thighs like watermelons and wear only Rapha kits and ride at a 25 mph pace, then their Saturday ride is your ride. Plus Meteor is a great bike shop (it’s a Canyon Experience Partner), and they serve strong espresso and tasty sourdough pizza.

No player, ever, has scored more points in her first two WNBA seasons. And no Dallas Wing, ever, has been a bigger boon to team business. She isn’t just the best athlete in town. She might be the most important, too.

It’s stunning to get this close to commercial jets as they land and take off. Plus the park’s speakers broadcast comms between pilots and air traffic control. On a recent morning, the woman controller greeted every arriving pilot with a cheer that made it sound like they were a family member arriving in her kitchen for breakfast.

The inaugural event, in July, in Deep Ellum, featured headliners Hanif Abdurraqib ( New York Times bestseller, long-listed for National Book Award in nonfiction) and Jamila Woods ( NPR’s Tiny Desk, CBS This Morning, The Late Show with Stephen Colbert ). Each gig was well attended and thoughtprovoking. More, please.

The Wings didn’t climb out of the WNBA cellar so much as explode out of it, setting a record for the league’s largest single-season turnaround. Paige Bueckers gets the bulk of the credit, but Dallas isn’t playoffbound without WNBA Most Improved Player Jessica Shepard and the returning Awak Kuier.

No matter what the Mustangs’ final record reads, 2026 is but another chapter in Lashlee’s five-season revival of SMU football, which includes the best three-year stretch in program history and the Mustangs’ first College Football Playoffappearance. Lashlee’s next task? Find a successor to Kevin Jennings, SMU’s greatest quarterback.

After a seven-year album drought, Ryan Bingham is having fun again. The depression and pain that most fans came to know him by from Crazy Heart has lifted. What’s left is a completely unlocked playbook thanks to his new partnership with The Texas Gentlemen.

n: GOOD LOCAL MARKETS AT FAIR PARK
b: Good Local Markets made its name in East Dallas but reached new heights after opening an outpost in Fair Park, smack in the middle of a food desert. The market brings in goods sourced within 150 miles and is also SNAPand WIC-certified, so South Dallas locals can purchase farm-fresh food in the spring and summer. Free parking at Gate 6.

Whether it’s their mini pancakes with ice cream and chocolate drizzle or a Taki crumb-coated elote, you’ll always be shocked (in a good way) by the generous toppings. Even more surprising is how they manage to pack so much freshly sliced mango into a cup.

We especially love Fruti’s dairy- based options such as the strawberries- andcream paleta—not overly sweet and even better when dipped in chocolate and rolled in nuts, something they’ll do with any of their pops.

There’s something for everyone at this McKinney institution, from fluffy bacon-cheddar scones to sticky-sweet kouign amann. Sourdough loaves look straight from the textbook, and Bresnan even bakes pizza by the slice. If you don’t want to drive north, they also sell at the Saint Michael’s Farmers Market.
a: 301 E. Louisiana St., Ste. B, McKinney. 214-578-1979.

b: Starship is becoming an ambassador for Dallas culture, taking its bagels to festivals in New York and winning awards against the East Coast’s finest. Its downtown location, next to the Giant Eyeball, is on many a tourist’s agenda. Seasonal specials keep getting more creative, too.
a: 1520 Elm St., Ste. 107. 469-772-9606; 6859 Arapaho Rd., Ste. 603. 469-864-7630. Multiple locations.

b: Fresh bread comes straight out of the oven at this Frisco bakery, and the crusty bread is the hero of the sandwich. The cold cut combination, loaded up with pâté and fresh veggies, is an ideal lunch for Texas summers and picnic weather alike.

The joy of a girl dinner is the spontaneity of building a haphazard plate. Slide into a bubblegum pink banquette, and let the staffhelp you and your gals (or snack-loving guys) put together a delightfully random spread. Sure bets: thick za’atar focaccia, in-house pastas, wagyu short rib, and chile-garlic broccoli.

Pho tai lan, a Northern Vietnamese specialty featuring a bounty of garlic and scallions, is the house favorite here. Pho Xom’s broths are deceptively simple and reflect hours of love in the kitchen. No wonder locals have taken to calling it “pho for purists.”
a: 2700 Old Denton Rd., Ste. 115, Carrollton. 214-731-6514. (Pictured: Tran Tran Nguyen, co-owner of Pho Xom)

b: The Grapevine institution is better than ever, with an expanded dining room that can finally accommodate its loyal followers. With a sandwich menu this long—more than 70 temptations—you should plan before you order. Chicago, New York, and Philly specialties are represented, along with Weinberger’s own indulgent inventions.

Filling dumpling wrappers with lamb birria is one of the many clever ideas at this ChineseMexican kitchen. The birria broth takes the place of the soup stock inside Chinese xiao long bao, adding a strong punch of fusion flavor. Order the “dumpling fiesta,” and your crispy pan-fried treats will arrive coated in a spicy dry rub.

The spirit of Italian cooking—seasonality, fresh produce, a bit of improvisation—is the guiding philosophy here. Pastas are always exemplary. If you don’t believe us, ask the hundreds of regulars who’ve helped keep Lucia thriving for 16 years.

This minichain with locations in Frisco and Irving claims to have some of the largest all-vegetarian dining rooms in the world. Everything on the enormous menu is worth ordering, and if decision fatigue strikes, the helpful staffwill offer recommendations. Rare specialty dosas and shikampuri (edamame) kebabs are highlights.
a: 13355 Main St., Frisco. 214-296-2190; 530 W. Lyndon B. Johnson Fwy., Irving. 469-994-7850.

b: This izakaya is so traditional and so beloved by Japanese expats that it can be hard to snag a seat. Sit at the bar and order drinking snacks, or take offyour shoes and sit on one of the floor cushions for a cozy group meal. Save room for green tea ice cream.

This newcomer brings glamour, a prestigious background (the chef was a UNESCO culinary ambassador), and superb dumplings. (Get the ultraflavorful green pepper xiao long bao.) Specialties from Shanghai and Taiwan appear next to top-quality teas, a blessing for city dwellers who often have to drive to the ’burbs for authentic Chinese cuisine.

Ichigoh has won this category for years on end despite a wave of competition. The ramen broths are always seasoned and balanced just right, and monthly specials keep the menu fresh. In summer, stay cool by going brothless.

A wise person once said that cookies are all about texture: getting those crispy, golden edges without sacrificing a gooey center. Nobody hits that note better than means there’s a treat for everyone’s taste. Leftover cookies are repurposed into world-class biscotti.

Their dreamy sesame-coated baguettes are the ideal accompaniment for a charcuterie-and-cheese night. The real gem, though, is sprouted quinoa loaf, which tastes like a nuttier, more flavorful version of whole wheat bread. Can’t decide? Sit down for a sandwich before you shop.

What was once a Detroit-style specialist is now a triple threat in East Dallas. Thunderbird still has its mighty Detroit pies, but if you want a thinner crust, you can also indulge in the city’s best New York-style pizza or a thin-and-crispy version that hails from the taverns of Massachusetts.

Name a restaurant after its patio, and you’d better deliver the square footage. The Yard, situated on an acre in downtown McKinney, does not disappoint. A canopy of oak trees supplies shade, and the 1,000-foot wraparound porch frames a historic home that dates back to 1878.

This well-rounded casual restaurant can fry a scrumptious piece of chicken, make a traditional shrimp pancake or fried rice bowl, and assemble some cheerfully unhealthy bar snacks. Most importantly, though, you can sample some of everything by taking advantage of three- and four-dish combo pricing.

The Lemon is a brilliant trick, a confection of white chocolate and lemon mousse, encased in a white chocolate shell that’s painted bright yellow and molded in the convincing shape of the yellow citrus fruit, complete with pedicel. If that sounds too fancy, dark chocolate cake is so fudgy that it’s practically molten.
st: Dallas 50 Best Restaurants Adds Georgie, Meridian, Tango Room

b: Mark your calendars, folks. This limited-run tribute to fast-food fish sandwiches is a Fond staple during Lent, and it makes very rare appearances the rest of the year. The kitchen fries thick sablefish fillets just right and bakes its own Japanese milk buns. It’s worth planning your year around.

From a humble truck parked east of Fair Park, sisters Gigi and Lenny Gomez Umanzor are quietly making a statement in Dallas’ booming matcha scene. The flavor of the ceremonial-grade green tea shines, and it can be further enhanced with seasonal additions. The sisters also offer creative takes on coffee standards and “refreshers,” from a lychee and strawberry Berry Bliss to a Minty Mara with mango and passion fruit.

The Turkish bakery expanded from an original standing-room-only commercial location into a thriving cafe and tea room. Order baklava at the counter, or sit at a table and watch the bakers at work through a window. A huge variety of flatbreads and pastries is all made from scratch.

n: GREEN POINT SEAFOOD AND OYSTER BAR
b: This is the kind of neighborhood restaurant that’s easy to dress up or down to any occasion. A quick, casual lunch over a bowl of chowder will be just as satisfying as dinner seafood towers, cioppino, and blackened redfish. Mini fish sandwiches make an extra-fun appetizer.

Mexican seafood is the specialty here, where chef Anastacia Quiñones- Pittman pays a sophisticated tribute to Baja’s bounty. Be sure to order some of the one- or two-bite appetizer snacks, adventurous creations that might be miniature tuna-caviar tarts, a single butter-poached scallop, or a crispy ceviche taquito.

c: Best Place to Celebrate an Anniversary
b: A new remodel has left The Charles darker, moodier, and more sophisticatedlooking than ever before. The kitchen has more swagger in its step, too. Dig into the Italy-focused wine list, celebrate with snow crab ravioli, and finish your night in the more private backroom bar.

Chef Kevin Ashade tells stories from the entire African diaspora at this downtown restaurant, which features spices and dishes from Jamaica, West Africa, and the American South. There’s sushi, too, but you’re best offstarting with suya skewers before feasting on jerk lamb shank or peri peri chicken.

Order the Puerco El Metro, a mixture of different cuts from a whole roasted pig folded into a tortilla and then garnished with fried pork skin, and ask for the Metro salsa, which balances creamy avocado with searing chile peppers. Or make a whole meal out of huesitos, salsa-coated rib tips.

Nobody else makes a fluffy tortilla like Gonzalez. The Oak Cliffand Pleasant Grove institution does all the classics right, including fried-to-order crispy tacos that are easily the best in the region. Ask for the salsa fresca, and skip the salsa that comes to your table automatically.

This small market is a treasure trove of specialty Asian items including Burmese fermented tea leaves, fried bean mix, and traditional clothing. The produce selection is small, but its gai choy and Thai eggplant are very fresh. Whole fish and Black Silkie chickens (with, yes, black skin) stock the freezers.

Look for noodle dishes advertised as “authentic,” including pad Thai with dried spices and bold flavors of lime, peanut, tamarind, and garlic chives. Boat noodles are terrific, and specialties from southern Thailand, where owner Fon Johnson grew up, can be knockout-level hot.

In an age of omakase bounty, Sushi Kozy stands out by virtue of variety. You’ll get a range of seafood, prepared with tradition and simplicity in mind, bookended by more creative kitchen dishes that combine French and Japanese technique. There’s nothing else like it in town.
st: Sushi Kozy Better Get That Michelin Star

b: Load up on the appetizer dips and fresh-baked pita breads, then order a lion’s mane mushroom grilled like a steak kebab, complete with chimichurri. (It also comes with lemony grilled sugar snap peas.) Don’t miss Halloumi cheese baked in a pastry crust and drizzled with honey.

There might not be a more romantic dining room in town than this candlelit art gallery, where you can sample foods that represent chef Wyl Lima’s globetrotting personal journey while admiring the paintings. Spike Lee recently bought a work from the walls. Next time he should stay for dinner.

This popular Greenville Avenue counter has an all-around menu of handrolls, nigiri, and sashimi. Look to the chalkboard for the daily specials of justflown-in fish. We especially appreciate the casual atmosphere and affordable price point, rare in town for sushi of this caliber.

It’s not TikTok hyperbole to say CNTRD’s smoothies are better than Erewhon. Stop in to the tiny, spartan space in Victory Park, order any of their seasonal smoothies, and receive a blended work of art that tastes as good as it looks.

Lauren Kitchens can make a cake that looks like a plate of oysters or Bevo in repose. You’ve probably seen the SMU (and Ursuline) grad’s work on Food Network and maybe at the occasional party thrown by Jerry Jones, Mike Modano, Don Henley, Jewel, or Blake Shelton and Gwen Stefani.

n: LA CASITA COFFEE AT HALF PRICE BOOKS
b: The wood-paneled cafe is great for intimate get-togethers (i.e., morning-after meals or BFF gossip fests). You’ll be jealous of your date’s choice, so agree to split dishes, such as the crispy potato sandwich and espresso-soaked French toast. After, get Turkish lattes to go and keep the convo going as you wind through bookstore aisles.

You know how the Grand Prairie Ikea is superior to the Frisco one because you can dash in and pick up a couple of picture frames and 10 pounds of salmon without walking 8 miles? The newest outpost of H Mart is like that. It’s got some of the freshest fish, produce, and meat in town, plus you can grab some chocorooms and a still-warm Spam musubi at checkout to snack on during the shorter drive home.

For more than four decades, this tiny but mighty Deep Ellum factory has produced award-winning cheeses, from mozzarella to queso Oaxaca to rosemary formaggio. The shop is stocked with just one refrigerator full of cheese, each handmade using fresh cow or goat milk. The ancho chile caciotta is divine.

The ice cream only needs to be so good when $4 buys you a single scoop that rivals most shops’ double. It just so happens that Tongue in Cheek’s also tastes outstanding. The Peanut Butter Buckeye Brownie is a crowd favorite, but save room for the decadent banana pudding flavor, too.
a: 526 W. Arapaho Rd., Richardson. 972-685-5070; 3505 E. Park Blvd., Ste. 300, Plano. 469-661-8001. Multiple locations.

b: Many of the city’s coffee veterans, who have storied careers managing, roasting, or serving for Dallas shops, have landed at Buzz. They roast in-house and source beans from the Women Producer Program of ARGCAFEE, which supports women in the coffee industry. Those brews fuel the many laptop-toting worker bees who fill the spacious shop.

Everything at this Vietnamese-owned spot is fried to order, resulting in hot, crispy chicken best paired with their coleslaw and mac and cheese. Hand-battered and fried in peanut oil, the thick breading on the wings and tenders is well seasoned and packs a crunch worthy of a viral TikTok mukbang.

Perhaps its location at the side of an interstate keeps Smokey Joe’s from developing the long lines and online fans common at more famous spots. The ribs would be enough to convert any skeptic, though. And the brakes, a South Dallas tradition of spiced rib trimmings, got their own moment in the sun this year after praise from James Talarico.

Dallas’ must-try burger map is full of smashed-into-lace patties, enough of them that an unpressed brisket-chuck, book-thick burger, grilled over hickory wood fire, feels momentous. Once your two-handsrequired monster arrives, press down to push the caramelized onion and zippy horseradish pickles into the beef.

We’re full of admiration for the sausage links here, packed with flavor without extra grease. We also love the steaks, pork chops, duck breasts, and house-made red and green chorizos. The vacuum-sealed cured meats are our go-to for no-fuss dinner parties.

n: THE CAPRESE AT LITTLE HERON BAKERY
b: This being a bakery, you shouldn’t be surprised that the sandwich starts with a pillowy hunk of focaccia best described as “We don’t need no stinkin’ side of chips”-sized. You’ll keep ordering it because Little Heron puts just as much care into what’s between the bread.

In a city full of high-falutin teas (see: The French Room, Mirador, Dior), this quaint, yellow Bishop Arts teahouse has been offering everyday Dallasites a sweet, sunlit afternoon experience for three decades. The chinoiserie sets remind us of Grandma’s house, and the BYOB policy is a bonus.

Co-owner Yaser Khalaf never had cold hummus from a tub in his native Kuwait. To replicate a true Middle Eastern experience here, his kitchen takes the labor-intensive step of blending every batch fresh to order. You can ask to add roasted veggies or cubed filet mignon on top.

Opened in 1961 by Karl Kuby, the eponymous shop now stocks hard-tofind imported goods in the market and serves a breakfast and lunch fit for the Honorary Consul of the Federal Republic of Germany in Dallas. That would be Nicola Bremer, who tells us she likes the house double-smoked pork chops.

Walk inside, and it looks like they plopped El Si Hay in the middle of a former donut shop. The walled-offkitchen has a small order window on one side and pickup window on the other. There are four choices, all with egg. Straightforward, convenient, made fresh, tasty, and inexpensive: everything a breakfast taco should be.

This greasy spoon has been slinging damn good food since 1972. Servers may act like stubborn grandfathers, but they will not let you leave dissatisfied. John’s giant biscuits should help on that front. We suggest you park far away; you’ll need to walk offbreakfast after leaving your table.

Be prepared to wait in line. Be prepared to pay more than $5 for a single donut. And be prepared for your mouth to go to heaven when you bite into a Cookies Butter Brioche donut that has been fermented and then fried in tallow, not the standard vegetable shortening.

When pastrami brisket is available on special at this iconic barbecue joint, ask for it in sandwich form. You’ll get a generous portion of smoked slices plus pickles and mustard, which are all the condiments you need to dress up some of the most flavorful meat in the whole state.

The kitchen inside Four Corners Brewing Company turns out terrific burgers, carne asada fries, and nachos. The Texas Sun boasts a frizzle of skinny grilled onions, spicy sauce, and crisp beef patties that hang out over the bun’s edges. We keep room in our grease-filled hearts for the all-chorizo smash.

One of the few local steakhouses committed to sourcing Texas ranch beef, Nuri is equally committed to luxurious surroundings and service. Bring a group to share a bone-in cut from HeartBrand and a few bottles from the top-of-class wine cellar.

We don’t talk enough about the spray tan gamble. When they turn out bad, you basically have to wear a potato sack until the stain fades. There is no such stress at Queen Bee. One D editor trusted them to airbrush on a natural tan two days before her wedding, with glowing results.

The designer mix is perfect. The layout is impeccable. And every purchase is a workhorse investment that will stand the test—and trends—of time. Only at Kick Pleat can you find Japanese Chimala jeans, Antwerp-adjacent knitwear, and Birkenstock’s luxury1774 line.

Whether we’re looking to relax following a stressful work week, celebrate a special occasion, or treat ourselves for no good reason at all, our RX is always the same: the Joule Spa. The moody subterranean space is where we leave our troubles for a few hours and emerge a new person.

This Bishop Arts shop carries just what the name suggests in the form of housewares, accessories, and bathand-body goodies. But what draws us in again and again is the assortment of sweet letterpress greeting cards befitting any special occasion (or for no occasion at all). Pair one with a gift, or let your message stand alone.

Former Estée Lauder Co. beauty exec Rachel Green and master perfumer Elena Ruiz launched the small-batch fragrance brand last year with the idea that signature scents are a myth. What we really need is a rotation of niche, high-quality scents based on our mood of the moment.

After opening in the Design District last year, this housewares store quickly expanded with a second location on Knox and the addition of a registry service. Nary a KitchenAid stand mixer here, but you will find exquisite Italian table linens, Swedish brass candlesticks, and Australian porcelain dinnerware, all exclusive to KD Biel.

Patricio Rivera is a sculptor who happens to work with flowers. His arrangements command a room, but what really sets him apart is the vessel. He knows the container matters just as much as the blooms and fills his shop with one-ofa-kind vases, including stunning pieces by local artists Barbara Harvel and Brooks Oliver.

Don’t let its humble exterior fool you. Nicholson-Hardie is much more than a gardening shop. With Nest candles, Assouline coffee table books, Steiffteddy bears, and the softest pajamas, it’s the first place we go when we need a sure-to-please gift for the snobs we know and love.

We have long appreciated the flagship’s “people’s store” aura: the tables full of retirees playing pickup mahj and undergrads cramming. But recently we’ve been gobsmacked by the events with blockbuster authors: Matt Dinniman of Dungeon Crawler Carl , and Annabel Monaghan, the witty romance queen. So litty, HPB.

It doesn’t have the most Instagrammable aesthetic of the pet shops in town, but Odyssey is the top dog when it comes to grooming services. The staffis knowledgeable, friendly, and happy to help with larger breeds other groomers won’t take. We love their adoption, educational, and philanthropic events, too.

Beyond its expansive offering of indoor and outdoor plants (we’re partial to its selection of natives), this shop can teach you a thing or two, too. Garden advisors take your dumbest questions seriously, and their classes cover everything from plant life cycles to growing wildflowers from seed. At-home coaching is also available.

The slogan “not your Mimi’s needlepoint” tells you all you need to know about Bishop Arts’ newest craft shop. The owners, Amelia and Madeline Alford (pictured right, a former D employee), started with their own Etsy line of millennial- and Gen Z-specific designs, and now that same breed of snarky, pop-culture, and internet-humor canvases is a specialty.

c: Best New Jewelry for the Fashion Forward
b: This Shops of Highland Park store has been curating pieces from rising jewelry designers for more than 35 years. Cases are full of bold, colorful, and fresh styles. Think oversize pendants and bright beads from names such as Jennifer Meyer and FoundRae. While the styles may be fashion-forward, every piece is heirloom quality.

If accessories are the jewelry of interior design, Mecox is your go-to home jeweler. With fresh inventory dropping constantly, Mecox entices you to swing by regularly, as the best pieces don’t stay long. Be sure to check out curated collections by local artists such as ceramics by Jim Tompkins and Paul Schneider.

This nearly 30-year-old Grapevine shop is alternately overrun with Easter bunnies, Uncle Sams, and skeletons, depending on the time of year. And while it earns its place in the heart of the self-proclaimed Christmas Capital of Texas each November and December, you can stop in any time of the year to shop holiday village displays in rear rooms.

c: Best Way to Say I Love You
b: Founder Rhonda Camp Warren’s selection of ready-made and semicustom stationery makes it fun to share (and receive) sentiments via snail mail. We also love the less traditional ways she enables you to express your love—with business-card-size “emoticards” or, if the way to their heart is through their stomach, charcuterie cheat sheets.

This Dallas-based e-commerce brand carries leather staples—purses, wallets, and luggage—plus fun extras like office goods and a new sporting collection. Pieces are easily customizable with plenty of colors and monogramming options, as well as the ability to emboss your own artwork or handwriting on a keepsake.

Friends Lauren Cooper and Kenzie Killgore translated their love for sourcing vintage art into an e-commerce-based gallery of secondhand finds. These aren’t no-name garage-sale scores; artist information is provided for each piece. Still, most of their inventory of oils on canvas—largely landscapes and still lifes—are snaggable for under $1,000.

n: THE CRESCENT HOTEL, FORT WORTH & CANYON RANCH
b: Hotel Crescent Court’s sister property to the west is cosmopolitan and comfortable without an ounce of cowboy kitsch. Book an overnight stay and score access to Canyon Ranch, a world-class wellness club that offers fitness classes, spa services, and holistic recovery experiences. Despite being just 30 miles from home, you’ll feel totally transported.

A few years into its Design District era, this former Henderson Avenue staple is offering the same great selection with extra room to flex. We are obsessed for one reason: where else can you leave with a $25,000 “priceless” piece in one hand and a $40 catchall in the other?

We’d gladly trade in our corner office (read: cubicle) for the trad-wife life if our kitchen was outfitted only in beautiful but functional wares from this downtown McKinney shop. In addition to handcrafted serving pieces, cookware, and kitchen tools, they stock small-batch pantry items, cool cookbooks, and organic cleaning products worthy of the hautest homestead.

Stop scrolling the big-box craft sites, and head to Paper Arts in Old East Dallas instead. Owner Terri Thoman has spent 40-plus years sourcing incredible papers from around the globe. Between the live origami demos and printmaking workshops, it’s pure tactile inspiration you’ll never get with online shopping.

Whether you buy it in-store or bring it from elsewhere, if you can physically gift it, the volunteers at this nonprofit shop can wrap it. They handle one-offpresents and corporate gifting needs with equal panache and precise corners, and they’ll get creative when paper won’t do.

From a sofa shaped like a giant stuffed bear to a desk crafted to resemble an oversize book, you never know what you’ll see at Scott + Cooner. While it peppers its showroom with unexpected conversation pieces, the store’s staples are sleek, modern classics from lines such as Cassina and de Sede.

You could argue that “Stay Fit Britt” Everett is Dallas’ own Tracy Anderson. The personal trainer also turned her fitness method into a multiplatform brand—just with more Pilates, strength, and sculpt than Anderson’s danceforward workouts. Everett’s first in-person studio is a stunning, and extremely challenging, representation of what she’s built.

When Highland Park’s iconic Mushroom House came down, we knew where to hunt for the salvaged treasure. Discount Home Warehouse is the ultimate demolition store. From one-of-a-kind vintage light fixtures and double doors packed with character to entire kitchens for your next big remodel, chances are they’ve got the scraps to complete your unique project.

Yes, infants outgrow clothes faster than you can say “insufficient funds.” But here are our two cents: dress your children in the finest, most fanciful garb you can before baggy t-shirts and Crocs become their uniform. Dondolo makes classic clothing that’ll make you nostalgic for the baby days, even when you’re still in them.

Ready to have the time of your life? Head to Scout Design Studio for some wild finds—from a stone bust of Patrick Swayze to a cigarette butt side table. Just remember: nobody puts these babies in a corner. Scout’s statement pieces are made to be front and center.

You can’t know how soft a onesie feels, if the pockets on that diaper bag will fit your preferred bottle brand, or how easily you can collapse that trendy stroller one-handed until you’ve touched, tried, and tested them in real life. This Snider Plaza mainstay helps new parents get confidently in gear.

Though this local institution recently opened its fourth North Texas location, in NorthPark Center, our fave is still the original Preston Royal shop. The selection is expansive but not overwhelming, stocked with a delightful mix of classic and trending toys for all ages and interests.
a: 6025 Royal Ln., Ste. 223. 214-265-9971; 5600 W. Lovers Ln., Ste. 123. 469-250-7426. Multiple locations.

b: It’s safe to say Blue Print defines Dallas style. A mix of fun, colorful patterns and traditional shapes will make you on-trend today and timeless tomorrow. It has two Dallas locations (plus a gallery annex). You could easily walk in and furnish your entire home in one fell swoop.

In addition to adult classes and workshops highlighting an array of mediums, this 16-year-old creative haven offers weekly classes and camps for kids, ranging from teens to toddlers as young as 2. Options for the younger set include drawing, painting, collage, and loom weaving. Lessons are always engaging, enriching, and age-appropriate.

You don’t need to be a mid-century expert to shop here. Chris Thurman knows the story behind every single piece, from a Hans Wegner “China” chair to a giant leather rhinoceros bench by Valenti. Best of all, everything is restored so meticulously that it looks even better than the day it was made.

There are stores that have a wider selection, but this Preston Royal newcomer appeals to the Montessori-minded with a quality-over-quantity approach. Titles are thoughtful and thought-provoking, and the wood-wrapped reading room is just-right-size for little readers. Check out their new kids’ movie night series, too.

Brides and families look to Bell’Invito for masterful stationery in Dallas. Founder and etiquette expert Heather Wiese is best known for beautiful custom work: monogrammed, wedding, and holiday stationery especially. But procrastinators need not sacrifice quality. Equally elegant semicustom options are available in a pinch.

This downtown McKinney shop is super wholesome without feeling dated. Think Little House on the Prairie, but the Ingalls fam got a high-end designer makeover. Owners Rachel and Daniel Brasch bring their design-build expertise to a cozy space where you can pop in, grab a gift, and get inspired.
a: 211 E. Louisiana St., Ste. A, McKinney. 214-548-4582.

c: Best Place to Break the Mold
b: Shopping at this home-furnishings store is like walking through a gallery. It looks minimal at first, but you’ll spend hours obsessing over every detail; each piece is a literal work of art. We cheered when it opened in the Design District, filling a niche we were missing: something completely different.

Both the Oak Cliffand Design District locations live up to their “cool stufffor cool people” tagline. The booths at Lula B’s are packed with rare finds, so allot plenty of time to explore and dig. Keep up with their Instagram, where they post daily their new pieces.
a: 1010 N. Riverfront Blvd. 214-749-1929; 1982 Fort Worth Ave. 214-824-2185.

c: Best Reason to Have a Dinner Party
b: If your aesthetic happy place is the late ’80s, welcome home. Weston Table is packed with tartan, hunter green, burgundy, and rich woods. Think Ralph Lauren meets L.L.Bean, with a serious Match pewter situation—the entire collection is here. It makes setting the table for no reason at all feel like a good idea.

Founder Lindsey Adams Williams wanted fashion without compromising comfort. Her waterproof, hypoallergenic screw-back studs come in everyday shapes (hearts, flowers, pearls) and whimsical ones, too (Christmas trees, cowboy boots, snowflakes). And after a long day of looking so chic, the flat backs won’t poke you when you lay down your weary head.

As their t-shirts say, you can’t roll a joint on a digital download. This is where you go for vinyl (and CDs and tapes) and live in-store performances that truly create that overused word: community. When Leon Bridges dropped his latest album, he came here for a meet-andgreet. That’s Happiness Anytime.

The constellation of cool Dallas menswear stores gets a little bigger every year. The latest star to know: Cypress, a men’s- and unisex-focused collective by Cole Levine. Book a private or virtual appointment to shop the cult Scandinavian minimalist label Mfpen or selvedge denim by Yoko Sakamoto.

When she’s not napping with oversize babies at the elephant orphanage she co-founded in Botswana, Stevens is taking equal care both with priceless museum-size works of art and your twee Wipstitch needlepoint canvas. She has an impeccable eye for finding the treatment that makes each piece pop.

If flying commercial weren’t bad enough, now everyone and his mother has lounge access. P/S is the new semiprivate solve: a gorgeous, new terminal with its own TSA checkpoint, Champagne and caviar service, and private suites if the salon bar is still too public.

Alternative R&B on the speakers. Limewash on the walls. Vintage Ralph Lauren and fresh Momotaro denim on the racks. Shay Thompson’s downtown McKinney shop may be small, but the energy is strong. Go on the weekend to kick it with other dudes who care about what they wear.

“Print is dead,” said Egon Spengler in Ghostbusters , but this crew is proving him wrong. They offer the raw grit of true printmaking: the smell of fresh ink and the clatter of the letterpress and engraving machines. Plus, you can actually oversee your job on-site and make adjustments on the press in the print factory.

The Conservatory in Highland Park Village carries rare fragrance houses such as Maison d’Etto, Ex Nihilo, and Perfumehead. But the real draw is Shasa Mitcham, whom we dubbed “The Best Nose in Dallas.” His superpower is pinpointing your ideal scent before you even know what you’re looking for.

You could spend the whole day at this diner-by-day, music-venue-by-night Design District newcomer, which took over the Ferris Wheelers spot. The whole menu is a smash hit, but don’t miss the pozole grits. Once you’re fueled, head to the backyard to catch bands, musicians, or DJs playing in the moonlight.

It’s not day drinking if you’re reading a book. Besides, during happy hour, if you buy a book, your next drink is free. Take a seat inside the shop, on the front porch, or in the shady backyard, which, with its picnic tables and restful quiet, is ideal for reading. And the other thing.

The aviation theme fits On Rotation’s setting on the edge of Love Field. The split-level patio offers space for both kids and grown-ups. And the tap list is a wide-ranging mix of its own excellent beers and well-chosen guest brews. On Wednesday, beers running low are half price.

With a d&b Audiotechnik sound system, and a 108-linear-foot 4K video wall, and 32,000 square feet of rave space, this former grain silo has served as a local landing pad for electronic legends, including Tiësto, Diplo, Zedd, and Fatboy Slim. Discover up-and-comers inside Ductwork, the venue’s “techno speakeasy.”

This spring, a $20 million renovation revived the 103-year-old Uptown hotel. The lush, glamorous transformation vaulted The Stoneleigh into top Dallas hotel territory, but our favorite new feature may be Bar Leonessa’s Tiny Tini. Snag two for $13 during weeknight happy hours.

There’s no better fuel for a night of karaoke than a heaping platter of Korean fried chicken, some bulgogi quesadillas, and a few affordable bottles of soju. DanSungSa’s semiprivate booths and bumping soundtrack add ; 4:30 on Fridays and Saturdays.

DJ Alaska, aka Alaska Quiñones, is the face-painted ringmaster behind clown raves and a thriving subculture among Dallas alts and goths. The Oak Cliffpayasita mixes cumbias, rock, and hyperpop into electrifying sets, and she has taken her act to Atlanta, where she opened for Japanese DJ Yousuke Yukimatsu.

Lake Highlands’ favorite brewpub had a big year in 2026, collaborating with a Bolivian chef (a mocochinchi-spiced amber), Mississippi and Austin breweries (a hoppy pilsner and dark rice lager), and the Oak Cliff Film Festival (an oat lager). As for the saison aged in Malört barrels, hey, they’ll try anything.

What a great record store is to music, Strangeways is to beer. Yes, you can find some chart-toppers, but the joy comes from combing through the 40 beers on tap to find your groove among the hidden gems from many of the best breweries in and out of Dallas.

Rule of thumb: don’t order gravy at a dive bar. This Richardson mainstay is the exception, with a scratch kitchen that slathers the good stuffon chicken-fried steak as well as a mushroom-Swiss burger. But you need not eat to have a good time. The live music upstairs thumps, and the beer is cheap.

For such a small shop, this Oak Cliffgem has a little bit of everything. Topshelf Champagne for a classy soirée? They have it. An underappreciated $20 rosé? That, too. Funky natural wines and old-world classics sit side by side on the racks. If you can’t choose, sit down for a glass before shopping.

This Cowtown venue on the cusp of a name change hosted huge names in 2026, including Eric Church, Luke Bryan, Phoebe Bridgers, and Ella Langley, but the 14,000-seat space feels more intimate and less cavernous than other arenas. It’s also home to the largest L-Acoustics arena sound system. Translation: music just sounds better here.

Any of six outstanding cocktails runs you $9. Plunk down a few more bucks, and you get a meze trio featuring the best hummus in town, each batch made to order. And Zon Zon didn’t forget the wine drinkers: a bartender-selected bottle runs half price.

Set Misti Norris’ inventive mind loose on a bar, and you might wind up with a Southeast Asian hot dog, a cheffy cereal bowl for dessert, and chicken nuggets with serious culinary credentials. We won’t trigger your envy by telling you about the now-departed pastrami musubi.

Downtown’s new Mexican cantina takes the drinking snack seriously. With every round, your table will get a different morsel: spiced nuts, fresh fruit, a cup of broth. By all means, avail yourself of the traditional food menu, too, but the warm hospitality of these botanas will stick in your memory.

Matchbooks are all the rage in personalized home decor lately (sure, why not?), and this Plano restaurant offers the most whimsical of all. Retro illustrations aren’t just on the front and back of the matchbook, but also on each individual match. Only downside: you’ll never want to light them.

The punny name doesn’t lie. Your phone’s camera will be blinded when the bouncer tapes it upon entry. That’s the point: take a break from the screen, and dance like no one can see you on Snapchat. Cuz they can’t.

Two of these ’tinis will have you buying The Charlotte’s signature teddy bears offthe menu. Yes, the porn star martini is strong, but deliciously sweet, thanks to the restaurant’s twist on the London classic—a dash of pineapple juice enhancing the usual concoction of vanilla vodka and passion fruit liqueur.

Each holiday season, the bars on Bishop Lane transform into an interconnected, over-the-top winter wonderland with twinkling lights, thousands of ornaments hanging on every spare surface, and mini (inedible) presents in cocktails. The life-size Elf on the Shelf at the entrance is positioned perfectly for photos in his embrace.

This Uptown pub doesn’t just provide an emcee pushing play on karaoke tracks. Every Thursday night, a live band posts up to back all the wannabe Lindsey Buckinghams, Taylor Swifts, and Freddie Mercurys. Performers, beware: you’re not just background noise for this crowd; they expect you to entertain.

Drop by during the day for a soothing thermal circuit (sauna, cold plunge, hot spring). Or drop by at night to do it all with cocktails and a bit more socializing. There are a variety of ways to experience WorldSprings, but they all help with circulation.

The backbar library of tequila, mezcal, sotol, raicilla, and other Mexican spirits should rank as a local landmark and tourist attraction. It’s one of the most impressive collections in the United States. But if you’re intimidated, you can sample the clever, refreshing cocktails.

Entering The Statler’s sultry basement spot feels like an illicit, Prohibition-era rendezvous, where the martinis are just as smooth as the pipes of the live jazz singer. Whether you’re on a date with your boo or your besties, your night will find life in the haze of dim lighting and a tobacco Old Fashioned.

The Bishop Arts music venue is known for lively jazz performances, but its cocktail menu deserves applause, too. Its offthe-menu carajillo, a Mexican-inspired alternative to the espresso martini, combines rich coffee and mezcal beneath an exceptionally creamy foam. Check the calendar online to pair your cocktail with live tunes.

Gunpowder Gin, sunset-hued house-made tonic, a strip of grapefruit zest, and a makrut lime leaf: the Mansion’s house G&T is iconic. So is its equestrian-themed setting with its handcarved fireplace. Add live Sinatra-style crooners on weekends, and you can feel like a billion bucks for the price of a dry-aged burger.

This place debuted for the World Cup, and daytime lines formed to watch matches—in Deep Ellum! Justly so. The multiple interior spaces are comfortable. The Scotch egg has a perfectly tender yolk. The chips with the fish are a clever American twist. And the backbar once sat in the Green Room. IYKYK.

If the scene on the Oak Lawn strip overwhelms the senses, this dimly lit lounge serves as a coping strategy via cozy booths, stiffcocktails, and a happy hour “kid’s meal” that comes with a ciggie. Go for Girls and Gays night each Thursday, and get $12 martinis.

We have a friend whose Indian-born wife craves an Indian gin that practically no one in the United States has heard of. Our friend asked the fine folks at Pogo’s if they could find it for his wife’s birthday. Of course they could. GM Courtney Luscher and her staffare tops.

It bears repeating: 27,000 square feet; 30 mature live oaks; a Texas country playlist built by a human, not an algorithm; servers schlepping impossible pyramids of frosty beer schooners; and the one thing that no other patio has: scantily clad gals and shirtless guys parading by on the Katy Trail. Eyes peeled for Troy Aikman.

In this subterranean audiophile haven, DJs spin vinyl with pure haki , and the beat pounds your chest before it hits your ears, thanks to the custom OJAS sound systems. Sip a highball and have a soft serve in the cerulean, velveteen vault, or hit the dance floor and bow to the bass.
st: Downtown Dallas’ Newest Bar ShyBoy Is a Hi-Fi Listening Haven
